Every state has the same number of electors as it has congresscritters: 2 senators and some number or representatives. The number of representatives changes every 10 years, based on the census. State lines rarely get redrawn. (States were conceived of as separate countries -- and yes some did have state religions -- which negotiated with each other in a UN-like federal government. Now, all this has changed since... 1820?, but that's the backdrop of how the electors work.) The important part to notice here are the two electors which correspond to the Senators. These are NOT representative of population, but rather the state as an administrative entity. This helps the electoral vote go against the popular vote. (There's also a possibility of that given distributed means, but it's statistically irrelevant.)

Within the states, gerrymandering can solidify representational districts. This does not change how many districts you have, only the homogeneity of voters within the district. You can make a district a stronghold or battleground. Or, as was the case of Gary Condit, you can use declining populations to edit people out of the picture. Redrawing these districts doesn't change anything in the Electoral College.

There is something to be said about population centers. Mostly, that these are the most easily stacked votes, but they often become their own districts. In this way, the House of Representatives can become a rigged deal. Senators? Well, they're not supposed to be elected by the populace. FDR changed that.
